{{short description|Nonlinear time delay differential equation}}
In [[mathematics]] and [[mathematical and theoretical biology|mathematical biology]], the '''Mackey–Glass equations''', named after [[Michael Mackey]] and [[Leon Glass]], refer to a family of [[delay differential equation|delay differential equations]] whose behaviour manages to mimic both healthy and pathological behaviour in certain biological contexts, controlled by the equation's parameters.<ref name="mackey-glass">{{cite journal|author1=Mackey, M.C.|author2=Glass, L.|year=1977|title=Oscillation and chaos in physiological control systems|journal=Science|volume=197|issue=4300|pages=287–9|doi=10.1126/science.267326|pmid=267326|bibcode=1977Sci...197..287M}}</ref> Originally, they were used to model the variation in the relative quantity of mature [[blood cell|cells]] in the blood. The equations are defined as:<ref name="mackey-glass"></ref><ref name="wolfram">{{WolframDemonstrationsProject |title=Mackey-Glass equation |urlname=MackeyGlassEquation |access-date=10 August 2020 }}</ref>
{{NumBlk|:|<math>
  \frac{dP(t)}{dt} = \frac{\beta_0 \theta^n}{\theta^n + P(t - \tau)^n} - \gamma P(t)
</math>|Eq. 1}} 
and
{{NumBlk|:|<math>
  \frac{dP(t)}{dt} = \frac{\beta_0 \theta^n P(t - \tau)}{\theta^n + P(t - \tau)^n} - \gamma P(t)
</math>|Eq. 2}} 
where <math>P(t)</math> represents the density of cells over time, and <math>\beta_0, \theta, n, \tau, \gamma</math> are parameters of the equations.

Equation ({{EquationNote|2}}), in particular, is notable in [[dynamical systems]] since it can result in [[chaotic attractor|chaotic attractors]] with various dimensions.<ref name="kantz">{{cite book|author1=Kantz, H.|author2=Schreiber, T.|year=2004|title=Nonlinear time series analysis|volume=7|publisher=Cambridge University Press}}</ref>

==Introduction==
[[File:Mackey-glass stable timeseries.png|thumb|400px|Time series generated from the Mackey–Glass equations. This can be seen as modelling a healthy variation of blood cell density. Here, <math>\tau = 6</math>.]]
[[File:Mackey-glass unstable timeseries.png|thumb|400px|Also generated from the Mackey–Glass equations, but now could be seen as pathological blood cell density variation. Here, <math>\tau = 20</math>.]]

There exist an enormous number of [[physiology|physiological systems]] that involve or rely on the periodic behaviour of certain subcomponents of the [[system]].<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Glass, L.|year=2001|title=Synchronization and rhythmic processes in physiology|journal=Nature|volume=410|issue=6825|pages=277–84|doi=10.1038/35065745|pmid=11258383|bibcode=2001Natur.410..277G|s2cid=4379463}}</ref> For example, many [[homeostasis|homeostatic processes]] rely on [[negative feedback]] to control the concentration of substances in the blood; [[respiratory center|breathing]], for instance, is promoted when the brain detects high CO<sub>2</sub>  levels in the blood.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Specht, H.|author2=Fruhmann, G.|year=1972|title=Incidence of periodic breathing in 2000 subjects without pulmonary or neurological disease|journal=Bulletin de physio-pathologie respiratoire|volume=8|issue=5|pages=1075–1083|pmid=4657862}}</ref> One way to model such systems mathematically is with the following simple [[ordinary differential equation]]:
:<math>
  y'(t) = k - c y(t)
</math>
where <math>k</math> is the rate at which a "substance" is produced, and <math>c</math> controls how the current level of the substance ''discourages'' the continuation of its production. The solutions of this equation can be found via an [[integrating factor]], and have the form:
:<math>y(t) = \frac{k}{c} + f(y_0) e^{- c t}</math>
where <math>y_0</math> is any initial condition for the [[initial value problem]].

However, the above model assumes that variations in the substance concentration is detected immediately, which often not the case in physiological systems. In order to ease this problem, {{harvp|Mackey, M.C.|Glass, L.|1977}} proposed changing the production rate to a function <math>k(y(t - \tau))</math> of the concentration at an earlier point <math>t - \tau</math> in time, in hope that this would better reflect the fact that there is a significant delay before the [[bone marrow]] produces and releases mature cells in the blood, after detecting low cell concentration in the blood.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Rubin, R.|author2=Strayer, D.S.|author3=Rubin, E.|year=2008|title=Rubin's pathology: clinicopathologic foundations of medicine|publisher=Lippincott Williams & Wilkins}}</ref> By taking the production rate <math>k</math> as being:
:<math>
\frac{\beta_0 \theta^n}{\theta^n + P(t - \tau)^n} ~~ \text{ or } ~~ \frac{\beta_0 \theta^n P(t - \tau)}{\theta^n + P(t - \tau)^n}
</math>
we obtain Equations ({{EquationNote|1}}) and ({{EquationNote|2}}), respectively. The values used by {{harvp|Mackey, M.C.|Glass, L.|1977}} were <math>\gamma = 0.1</math>, <math>\beta_0 = 0.2</math> and <math>n = 10</math>, with initial condition <math>P(0) = 0.1</math>. The value of <math>\theta</math> is not relevant for the purpose of analyzing the dynamics of Equation ({{EquationNote|2}}), since the [[change of variables|change of variable]] <math>P(t) = \theta \cdot Q(t)</math> reduces the equation to:
:<math>
  Q'(t) = \frac{\beta_0 Q(t - \tau)}{1 + Q(t - \tau)^n} - \gamma Q(t).
</math>
This is why, in this context, plots often place <math>Q(t) = P(t) / \theta</math> in the <math>y</math>-axis.

==Dynamical behaviour==
[[File:Mackey-Glass Attractors for Various Tau.gif|thumb|350px|Mackey–Glass attractors for various values of the parameter <math>\tau</math>]]

It is of interest to study the behaviour of the equation solutions when <math>\tau</math> is varied, since it represents the time taken by the physiological system to react to the concentration variation of a substance. An increase in this delay can be caused by a [[pathology]], which in turn can result in chaotic solutions for the Mackey–Glass equations, especially Equation ({{EquationNote|2}}). When <math>\tau = 6</math>, we obtain a very regular periodic solution, which can be seen as characterizing "healthy" behaviour; on the other hand, when <math>\tau = 20</math> the solution gets much more erratic.

The Mackey–Glass [[attractor]] can be visualized by plotting the pairs <math>(P(t), P(t - \tau))</math>.<ref name="wolfram" /> This is somewhat justified because [[delay differential equation|delay differential equations]] can (sometimes) be reduced to a system of [[ordinary differential equations]], and also because they are approximately infinite dimensional [[map (mathematics)|maps]].<ref name="kantz" /><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Junges, L.|author2=Gallas, J.A.|year=2012|title=Intricate routes to chaos in the Mackey–Glass delayed feedback system|journal=Physics Letters A|volume=376|issue=30–31|pages=2109–2116|doi=10.1016/j.physleta.2012.05.022|bibcode=2012PhLA..376.2109J|doi-access=free}}</ref>
